title: Stakeholder Communication & Lifecycle Management
intro: This domain covers the consulting half of the architect's job: discovering what a business actually needs, communicating decisions and trade-offs so different audiences can act on them, keeping expectations and SLAs anchored to evidence, documenting systems so others can build and run them, and stewarding an engagement through its full lifecycle. Exam questions here are scenario-based judgment calls — a stakeholder says or asks for something problematic, and you must choose the response that balances honesty, evidence, and relationship. Expect distractors that avoid hard conversations, over-promise, or jump to solutions before problems are defined.

objectives.objective: Conduct structured discovery and requirement gathering
objectives.explanation:
Discovery is the phase where the architect replaces assumptions with facts before any design work begins. Structured discovery starts from the business problem, not the requested technology: when a stakeholder asks for 'a chatbot' or 'an agent,' the architect's first move is to elicit the problem behind the request and the business metric a solution would need to move — cost per case, cycle time, resolution rate, revenue per interaction. A request is a hypothesis about a solution; discovery tests whether the underlying problem justifies it and whether a different solution fits better.

Three lines of inquiry anchor the phase. First, the target metric: what will change, how is it measured today, and what movement would count as success. Second, the current workflow and data reality: how the work is done now, where the exceptions and edge cases live, and whether the data the solution depends on actually exists in usable form — a stakeholder's claim that 'everything is documented' is a belief to verify, not a fact to design on. Third, the stakeholder map: sponsor, end users, IT, security, compliance, and legal each hold requirements and veto power, and any group missing from discovery will reappear later as a blocker.

Good discovery also separates stated wants from underlying needs. When an operations leader asks to 'automate every email,' the underlying need is usually to reduce handling load, and workflow data often shows a high-volume templated majority worth automating and a sensitive minority that should stay with humans. Finally, discovery closes by writing down measurable success criteria and explicit non-goals with the sponsor. 'We'll know it when we see it' is not a success criterion; it is a guarantee of later disappointment. Non-goals matter as much as goals because they are the reference point for every future scope conversation.
objectives.whyItMatters: Every downstream phase inherits discovery's quality. A solution scoped to the wrong problem cannot be rescued by good engineering, missing stakeholders resurface as launch blockers instead of requirements, and undefined success criteria mean the pilot gets judged against each stakeholder's private, unstated standard. Most failed AI engagements trace back to discovery shortcuts, not technical mistakes.

examples.title: The chatbot request that was really a cost problem
examples.body: A retail CEO opens a kickoff with 'build us a chatbot like ChatGPT.' Instead of sketching architecture, the architect asks what business pain prompted the idea. The answer: customer-service costs rose 40% and wait times are hurting reviews. Workflow mapping shows 60% of contacts are order-status queries the existing systems can answer via API. The right first solution turns out to be a narrow order-status assistant with a measurable target — deflect 40% of contacts — not a general chatbot. Problem-first elicitation found a smaller, higher-confidence project with a metric attached, and the CEO got a business case instead of a technology demo.

examples.title: Verifying the 'well-documented' policy corpus
examples.body: A benefits agency wants an assistant answering caseworker policy questions and assures the architect that 'all policy is documented.' Before proposing a design, the architect audits the actual sources and finds three generations of overlapping memos, scanned PDFs with no dates, and two regional variants that contradict each other. Discovery output shifts: the engagement now includes a corpus-curation workstream and a defined authoritative-source policy before any retrieval design. Designing first would have produced a system that confidently retrieved contradictory guidance — and the failure would have been attributed to the AI, not the data.

pitfalls: Accepting the stakeholder's requested solution as the requirement — the request is a hypothesis, and taking it literally skips the problem the engagement exists to solve.
Gathering requirements only from the sponsor, so users, security, and compliance discover the project when it is too late to shape it and just in time to block it.
Designing on unverified data claims; 'we have all the data' is the assumption most often wrong in RAG-style engagements, and only firsthand inspection settles it.
Leaving success criteria vague ('make it feel smoother') — without measurable criteria and explicit non-goals agreed before design, every later evaluation becomes a matter of taste.
Treating a prototype as a discovery tool for executives; a demo built before the problem is understood anchors expectations to the wrong thing convincingly.

objectives.explanation:
An architectural decision is not finished when it is made; it is finished when every audience that depends on it can act on it. The core skill is tailoring the framing to the audience while keeping the substance identical. Executives need the decision expressed in value, cost, and risk — hours saved, error exposure, cost per case — because those are the terms in which they weigh choices. Engineers need the technical rationale — why this pattern, what alternatives lost, what constraints bound the design. Auditors and security reviewers need traceability and evidence. Presenting latency percentiles to a CFO or value framing to an implementation team is the same mistake in opposite directions.

Trade-offs should be quantified, not asserted. 'The smaller model is probably fine' and 'cheaper but somewhat less capable' are not communicable positions; a measured comparison — accuracy delta, cost delta, latency delta from an eval run — is. Quantification does more than inform: it converts stakeholder conflicts into decisions the business can own. When a CFO wants the cheapest model and a product VP wants the best one, the architect's job is to price the quality-cost curve and facilitate a joint choice on it, not to referee the argument by personal preference.

Decisions also need durable form. A decision record capturing the options considered, why each was rejected, and the conditions under which the choice should be revisited turns reasoning into an organizational asset that outlives meetings and staff turnover. Finally, honest communication includes limitations. LLM systems are non-deterministic and their error rates are never zero; an architect who lets a stakeholder claim otherwise — in a board deck, a sales contract, or a press release — is trading long-term credibility for short-term comfort, and the debt always comes due when the first error surfaces.
objectives.whyItMatters: In production organizations, decisions get relitigated by people who were not in the room, executives fund what they can weigh, and auditors examine what was written down. Unquantified trade-offs produce decisions nobody owns, undocumented ones get reversed by accident, and overstated capabilities collapse trust the first time reality disagrees. Communication quality is what makes an architecture survive its own organization.

examples.title: One decision, three framings
examples.body: A hospital architect chooses RAG over fine-tuning for a clinical-guidelines assistant. For the executive committee: guidelines change monthly, RAG updates same-day at low cost while fine-tuning would lag weeks and cost more per update — lower clinical risk, lower run cost. For engineering: a decision record with the comparison matrix, rejection rationale for fine-tuning, and revisit triggers (e.g., if guideline churn drops or latency budgets tighten). For compliance: source-grounded answers are traceable to the current guideline version, supporting audit. Same decision, three artifacts, each audience able to act.

examples.title: Pricing a stakeholder standoff
examples.body: A retailer's CFO demands the cheapest model for product descriptions while merchandising demands the best, and both tell the architect to 'just decide.' The architect runs the three candidate models against brand-voice eval criteria and presents the curve: the cheapest model fails brand-voice checks 18% of the time, the premium model 3%, the middle model 6% at 40% of the premium cost. Framed that way, the executives converge on the middle model in one meeting — not because the architect chose for them, but because the trade-off finally had prices on it.

pitfalls: Presenting technical depth to executives (or value framing to engineers) — one framing pitched at the wrong altitude serves nobody, and the fix is translation, not glossaries.
Communicating trade-offs qualitatively ('faster but pricier') — unquantified trade-offs cannot be weighed, so the decision silently defaults to whoever argues loudest.
Announcing decisions without recording alternatives and rejection rationale, guaranteeing the choice is relitigated from scratch by every future skeptic.
Softening or omitting limitations to protect stakeholder confidence — LLM error rates are never zero, and hidden limitations surface as broken trust rather than managed risk.
Resolving stakeholder conflicts by personal judgment or diplomatic compromise instead of pricing the disagreement with evidence and letting the business choose.

objectives.objective: Manage stakeholder feedback loops and expectation alignment (including SLAs)
objectives.explanation:
Expectations drift toward whatever stakeholders last saw, and what they usually see first is a demo. A scripted demo on curated inputs shows what a system can do, not what it reliably does, so the architect's recurring task is re-anchoring expectations to measured baselines: eval results on representative data, expressed as ranges, with the conditions that produce the low end named. When a stakeholder demands a guarantee no LLM system can honestly give — '100% accuracy' — the move is not refusal or capitulation but redirection: present the measured range and design the end-to-end workflow (confidence routing, human verification) so the system meets the standard even though the model alone cannot.

SLAs are expectation management with contractual teeth, which means they must be derived from measured performance, not from sales enthusiasm. Latency commitments should reflect observed percentiles and, where whole-response latency is inherently long, use metrics that fit how LLM services behave — time-to-first-token with streaming, for example. Availability numbers must match the deployed topology. An architect asked to 'sign off quickly' on unmeetable numbers protects the client relationship by reworking the terms, not by annotating them.

Feedback loops are the mechanism that keeps expectations and reality converging after launch. Effective loops are structured: capture happens in the workflow at the moment of use and is linked to the specific case so it is actionable; a defined pilot cohort is accountable for participating; and a fixed review cadence turns the signal into decisions. Ad-hoc Slack complaints and after-the-fact surveys are not loops — they are noise with latency. The same evidence discipline governs both directions of stakeholder emotion: disappointment gets answered with the agreed baselines and improvement plan, and overexcitement — 'remove the human review, it clearly works' — gets tied to pre-agreed evidence gates such as sustained quality over a defined window and volume. Scope creep is expectation misalignment in slow motion; every 'small addition while you're in there' goes through explicit change control priced against timeline, cost, and the success criteria from discovery.
objectives.whyItMatters: Production systems live or die on the gap between what stakeholders expect and what the system measurably does. Unanchored expectations turn a 90%-accurate system into a perceived failure; unmeetable SLAs turn commercial wins into breach conversations; unstructured feedback lets pilots drift for weeks; and unmanaged enthusiasm removes safeguards faster than unmanaged disappointment cancels projects.

examples.title: From CEO demo euphoria to an evidence-gated launch
examples.body: After a flawless demo of a contract-review assistant, a SaaS CEO wants full launch in two weeks. The architect explains the demo used curated contracts and proposes instead: a four-week pilot with twelve design-partner customers, eval runs on a representative contract sample, and pre-agreed exit criteria — field-level accuracy above the agreed threshold across two consecutive weeks and pilot-user satisfaction above target. The CEO keeps a date to announce (pilot start), the launch decision becomes a measurement rather than an argument, and when the pilot surfaces a weak contract category, it is fixed before customers ever see it.

examples.title: Rewriting an SLA the architecture could not meet
examples.body: Sales drafts 99.95% availability and sub-second p99 for a document-analysis service that measures 4–9 seconds p99 on long documents from a single region. Rather than signing or stalling, the architect brings measured data to the SLA negotiation and reshapes terms: availability set to what the current topology supports with a roadmap-linked uplift, latency recast as time-to-first-token under 1.5 seconds with streaming plus a p95 completion bound per document size tier. The client gets commitments that will actually be honored — which, over a multi-year contract, is worth more than impressive numbers followed by credits and apologies.

pitfalls: Letting a demo set the production baseline — curated inputs and cherry-picked runs systematically overstate reliability, and the gap becomes stakeholder disappointment at pilot time.
Committing to SLA numbers the architecture has never measured, or using whole-response latency metrics for workloads where streaming metrics are the honest fit.
Promising or implying zero errors; the credible alternative is a measured accuracy range plus a workflow (confidence routing, human review) that absorbs residual error.
Collecting feedback through ad-hoc channels or lagging surveys instead of in-workflow, case-linked capture reviewed on a fixed cadence with a defined cohort.
Treating stakeholder overexcitement as harmless — early wins prompt demands to remove safeguards and scale prematurely, and only pre-agreed evidence gates convert that enthusiasm into a plan.
Absorbing 'small' scope additions informally to keep the sponsor happy, which silently diverges the sponsor's expectations from the delivery plan until they collide at launch.

objectives.objective: Document architectures and provide implementation guidance
objectives.explanation:
The test of architecture documentation is whether people who were not in the room can act correctly without the architect present. For a consulting architect this is literal: the engagement ends, and an engineering team that never met you must build and operate the system. A complete handoff package therefore covers four things — architecture and data-flow diagrams showing what moves where; prompt and configuration specifications; the decision rationale (what was considered, why it lost, what would reopen the question); and known risks with their mitigations. Rationale is the piece most often skipped and most expensive to lose: without it, the receiving team cannot distinguish load-bearing choices from incidental ones, and will 'improve' the former.

Documentation is a family of views on one system, matched to audience. Executives consume value-and-risk summaries; engineers consume component designs and interface contracts; security reviewers consume data-flow diagrams showing where sensitive data travels and which trust boundaries it crosses; operations consumes runbooks. A runbook maps observable symptoms to diagnostic steps, safe interim actions (fallback routing, disabling a tool), and escalation criteria — it is what lets a team that did not build the system respond at 2 a.m., and it is written before handoff because incidents do not wait for documentation sprints.

Two disciplines keep documentation trustworthy over time. First, prompts and configurations are behavioral source code and get version control treatment: change history, review before deploy, and traceability from each version to the eval results that validated it — so 'what is running and why' is a lookup, not archaeology. Second, documentation must be living: updating the affected docs is part of the definition of done for every change, not a quarterly ritual. Docs refreshed in batches are wrong most of the time and reconstructed from fading memory when finally fixed.
objectives.whyItMatters: In production, documentation is the difference between a system an organization owns and a system it merely hosts. Stale or missing docs turn every incident into archaeology, every new hire into a liability, and every departed architect into a single point of failure that already left. Security approvals, audits, and safe iteration all consume documentation — and consume it as it is, not as it was intended to be.

examples.title: The prompt-version incident that took a weekend
examples.body: A fintech's dispute assistant degrades on a Friday night. Three people had edited the system prompt directly in a dashboard over two months; nobody can say what is deployed, what changed, or what the prompt looked like when quality was last verified. The on-call engineer spends the weekend reconstructing behavior from logs. The remediation is not better people but better artifacts: prompts move into version control, changes require review and an eval run before deploy, and each version links to its eval results. The next quality dip is resolved in twenty minutes with a diff and a rollback target.

examples.title: A handoff package built for absence
examples.body: Rolling off a churn-briefing engagement, an architect has three weeks and limited documentation budget. Instead of a maximal spec, she prioritizes what the unknown receiving team cannot reconstruct: data-flow diagrams including the PII path, versioned prompt and retrieval configs with the evals that validated them, a decision log explaining why per-account retrieval beat batch summarization (and what scale change would flip it), and a known-risks list with mitigations. Six months later the team extends the system to a new data source correctly on the first attempt — because the rationale told them which constraints were load-bearing.

pitfalls: Documenting what was built but not why — without options-considered and rejection rationale, successors cannot tell load-bearing decisions from incidental ones and break the former.
Treating the architect's ongoing availability (calls, video walkthroughs, 'just ask me') as a substitute for a handoff package the team can execute unaided.
Leaving prompts and configs outside version control, so production behavior changes have no history, no review, and no link to the evals that justified them.
Handing operations diagrams and API references instead of runbooks — reference material describes the system, but only symptom-to-action procedures let an unfamiliar team respond to incidents.
Writing documentation once at design time and refreshing it in occasional sprints; docs stay true only when updating them is a required step of every change.

objectives.objective: Support lifecycle phases (discovery, design, handoff, monitoring, iteration)
objectives.explanation:
An AI engagement moves through discovery, design, build and pilot, handoff, monitoring, and iteration — and the architect owes each phase specific outputs. The sequencing matters because each phase's outputs are the next phase's inputs: design quality is bounded by requirement quality, pilot evidence depends on success criteria defined in discovery, and iteration depends on monitoring actually being reviewed. Under schedule pressure, phases compress rather than disappear: a one-week timeboxed discovery that verifies the metric, workflow, and data assumptions is legitimate; skipping to design because the client 'already knows what they need' is not, because the phase exists for its outputs, not its duration.

Handoff is a transition, not an event. A document drop — however complete — does not transfer the tacit knowledge of which behaviors are load-bearing. Effective handoff includes an overlap period in which the receiving team operates the system while the architect remains available, a defined support window, and a deliberate end so ownership actually transfers rather than becoming a permanent retainer dependency. Monitoring, similarly, is a practice rather than an artifact: dashboards without a scheduled review cadence, a named owner, and a route from findings into an iteration backlog produce exactly the failure they were built to prevent — measurable decline that nobody saw.

Iteration includes knowing its own limits. The recurring judgment call is tune versus redesign: prompt and configuration tuning fits when the problem is localized and fixes hold, but when repeated tuning decays quickly and analysis shows the workload has shifted outside the original design's assumptions — new inquiry types, new data domains, new users — that is the signal to loop back to design with the new reality as a discovery input. Finally, LLM systems have a lifecycle driver traditional software lacks: model versions deprecate on the vendor's schedule. A deprecation announcement starts the migration — run the existing eval suite against the successor, remediate regressions, re-certify if required, and cut over with buffer — because behavioral differences between model versions are discovered by evaluation, not absorbed by hope in the final month.
objectives.whyItMatters: Production AI systems fail as often from lifecycle neglect as from design flaws: discovery skipped under pressure produces well-built solutions to the wrong problem, handoffs done as document drops leave teams breaking their own systems, unreviewed dashboards let drift reach users before engineers, and unplanned model deprecations turn vendor calendar events into emergencies. Lifecycle discipline is what keeps a system valuable after the launch excitement ends.

examples.title: Tune or redesign: reading four failed tuning cycles
examples.body: A retail email assistant designed for pre-sale questions falls from 91% to 78% resolution. Four prompt-tuning rounds each recover a few points that erode within weeks. Analysis shows over half of current inquiries are post-purchase — orders, refunds, delivery — which the original corpus and workflow never covered. The architect reads the pattern correctly: decaying fixes plus a workload outside design assumptions means the design itself is stale. The team loops back to discovery-lite (characterize the new inquiry mix), extends the corpus and adds order-system tools in design, and resolution recovers durably — something no fifth tuning pass could have achieved.

examples.title: A deprecation clock treated as a project start
examples.body: A tax agency's citizen assistant runs on a model version with nine months to retirement, and the program manager wants to defer migration to month eight. The architect instead starts immediately: the certification eval suite runs against the successor model in month one and surfaces two behavioral regressions in edge-case tax guidance. Months two through four cover prompt remediation and re-certification; month five is a staged cutover with rollback available. When retirement arrives, the agency has been stable on the successor for months — versus the alternative timeline, where those same regressions would have been discovered with four weeks left and a certification process that takes six.

pitfalls: Skipping discovery when the client claims certainty — phases may compress under pressure, but their essential outputs (verified metric, workflow, data assumptions) cannot be skipped.
Treating handoff as a document drop; without an overlap period and defined support window, tacit knowledge never transfers and the receiving team breaks load-bearing behavior.
Equating monitoring with dashboards — measurement without a review cadence, an accountable owner, and a path into the iteration backlog is how declines go unnoticed until users complain.
Endlessly prompt-tuning a system whose workload has moved outside its design assumptions; fixes that decay while the traffic mix shifts are a redesign signal, not a tuning backlog.
Deferring model migration until a deprecation deadline is near, leaving no time for eval-driven regression discovery, remediation, and re-certification before forced cutover.
